title: CI, CD and CD
summary: What each practice promises, and where a human still presses a button.

steps.title: Why automate at all
body: Before CI, teams merged once a week and spent a day fixing what broke. "Works on my machine" was a real status report.
**Continuous integration (CI)** means every push is merged into the shared branch often (at least daily) and a server
**builds and tests it automatically**. The point is fast feedback: a broken build is found minutes after the change, while the
author still remembers what they did.
developer pushes ──► CI server ──► restore ► build ► test ──► ✔ green / ✘ red (author notified)
> **Tip:** CI is a team habit first and a tool second. A CI server that runs on a branch nobody merges for a month is not CI.

steps.prompt: A team runs a full build and test suite on a server, but only on a long-lived `develop` branch that is merged to `main` once a month. What are they missing?
options: Integrating often: the feedback is still a month late
steps.explain: CI is about integrating small changes frequently. Automation on a branch that rarely merges still hides conflicts for weeks.

steps.title: Delivery vs deployment
body: Both are abbreviated **CD**, which causes endless confusion:
| Practice | Every green change on main is... | Who releases to production |
| Continuous **delivery** | packaged and deployed to staging; *releasable at any moment* | a human clicks **Approve** |
| Continuous **deployment** | deployed all the way to production | nobody, the pipeline does |
Delivery:    commit ► build ► test ► package ► staging ► [manual approval] ► production
Deployment:  commit ► build ► test ► package ► staging ► production
Continuous deployment needs more trust in your tests and monitoring, because no human looks before users do.

steps.prompt: Which practice does each statement describe?
items: Every push triggers a build and the unit tests
A broken main branch is the team's top priority
Production releases need a person to approve them
Main is always in a releasable state, released on a business decision
A merged pull request reaches users with no human step
Bad changes are caught by automated checks and monitoring, not by a release manager

steps.prompt: A pipeline prints one line per decision. Tests passed on `main` and the team practises continuous **delivery**. What is the last line?
steps.explain: With continuous delivery the release to production waits for a person. Under continuous deployment it would say `deployed`.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: the automated path a change takes from commit to production
turning source code into something runnable
every check in the run passed
the shared main branch everyone integrates into

steps.prompt: Put the continuous delivery flow in order.
lines: Developer pushes a commit to main
Pipeline builds and runs the tests
Pipeline packages the build into an artifact
The same artifact is deployed to production
steps.explain: Note the last line: production gets *the same artifact* that was tested in staging, not a fresh build.

steps.title: What happens next?
prompt: Write `string NextAction(string branch, bool testsPassed, string practice)`. `practice` is `"delivery"` or `"deployment"`.
- tests passed but the branch is not `main` → `"ci-only"` (feature branches are checked, not shipped)
starter: string NextAction(string branch, bool testsPassed, string practice)
solution: string NextAction(string branch, bool testsPassed, string practice)
hints: Check the failure case first: nothing else matters if tests failed.
Then the branch, then the practice.
template: Dojo.Eq("failing tests stop everything", "stop", NextAction("main", false, "deployment"));
Dojo.Eq("feature branch only runs CI", "ci-only", NextAction("feature/login", true, "deployment"));
Dojo.Eq("main + delivery waits for a person", "await-approval", NextAction("main", true, "delivery"));
Dojo.Eq("failing feature branch stops", "stop", NextAction("feature/x", false, "delivery"));
